newsitem.title: FRANCE: CADES French franc bond issue helped by spread.
newsitem.headline: CADES French franc bond issue helped by spread.

text.p: French welfare debt repayment fund CADES staged a relatively successful return to the franc market, helped by somewhat generous pricing, traders said.

CADES issued 12 billion francs of 6.0 percent 2005 bonds at a spread of seven basis points over OATs, at the upper end of expectations, and syndicate members said there was reasonable demand from domestic and some non-resident investors.
"It must be said the spread, seven points over the government bond curve, was welcomed by everybody, the syndicate banks and investors alike," said one syndicate manager.
The Treasury, which oversees the CADES fund "made a gesture towards investors in view of the (recent) sharp decline in bond yields," said another banker in Paris.

Lead managers Banque Nationale de Paris and Credit Agricole had said on Wednesday the issue was to be priced with a spread of between five and seven basis points and one trader said the consensus among syndicate banks yesterday afternoon was six.

However a rally in the Matif December bond future early on Wednesday, which sent the contract to its highest levels this year, prompted a widening of the spread to seven to encourage investors to buy the paper, the trader said.
"This price attracted other potential investors," he said.

Although both the 2002 and 2007 bonds CADES sold in May were also initially priced at seven basis points over government bonds, traders said a narrower spread would have been possible for the 2005 bond given how well the existing paper was trading.
One banker at a French house, who had feared the issue would run into trouble, said in the end it had met with reasonable demand with some unexpected interest out of London.
"The salesmen certainly aren't pulling their hair out," he said.

The majority of the syndicate banks contacted said they had placed most of their allocations, some said all, although one dissenting syndication manager at a French bank said he doubted this was the case.

The overall impression given by the syndicate banks was that most of the demand came from domestic insurance companies and asset management divisions of French banks. The fact that much of the paper had been pre-placed certainly helped.
Still, some said between 10 to 15 percent of the paper went to foreign buyers in Germany, Britain, the United States and at least two central banks, one in northern Europe and one in the Middle East.
-- Yann Le Guernigou and David Clarke, Paris Newsroom +331 4221 5542
